metadata.description: PYQ-to-node curation artifact. One entry per pyq_id as curated. PYQs not yet curated are absent.
metadata.criterion: Link nodes for every concept the question surfaces (correct answer + distractors + context) — the interface is a study surface, not just a coverage proof.

schema.nodes: flat array of node_id strings covering answer + distractor + context concepts surfaced by the question
schema.status: covered (all surfaced concepts have nodes) | partial (answer has a node, some distractor/context does not) | uncovered (answer itself has no node)
schema.note: optional prose — human-readable gap description for partial/uncovered
schema.missing_concepts: optional for partial/uncovered — flat array of short concept names that need nodes; inverted by build_audit.py into audit_gaps.md (concept → PYQs)

10.resolved_note: hist_shankaradeva covers the Assam Vaishnavite tradition that birthed Sattriya (namghars, Eka Sarana Nama Dharma). No dedicated Sattriya (Sangeet Natak Akademi classical dance form) node, no explicit treatment of Borgeets / Ankia Nat / Bhaona — required to judge statement 3 (Tulsidas/Kabir/Mirabai attribution is false; Sattriya uses Shankardeva/Madhavadeva Borgeets).

14.resolved_note: Tribhanga pose had no dedicated node; drafted gap_tribhanga_pose (ancient-classical candidate) with distinction from Samabhanga/Abhanga/Atibhanga and PYQ-trap distractors (NOT a facial expression or hand-gesture concept).

missing_concepts: National School of Drama set up by Sangeet Natak Akademi (1959)
Sahitya Akademi Fellowship as highest honour conferred on a writer
19.note: Akademi nodes capture founding dates + mandate; NSD-as-sub-institution (1959) and Fellowship-as-apex-honour specifics missing.

missing_concepts: Article 18(1) and Bharat Ratna / Padma awards as not-titles (Balaji Raghavan 1995)
Padma Awards institution (1954) + suspensions (1977-80, 1992-97)
Bharat Ratna cap of three awards per year
38.note: Only era-11 recipient list exists; rules/history around titles, Padma suspension, annual caps are unanchored.

missing_concepts: International Mother Language Day (UNESCO, 21 February)
Bangla Language Movement + demand in Pakistan Constituent Assembly (Dhirendranath Datta, 1948)
39.note: Neither UNESCO IMLD nor the Bangla-language movement has any node. Uncovered.

40.resolved_note: Three tradition-community pairings had no nodes. Drafted composite gap_traditions_community_pairs covering all three (Chaliha Sahib-Sindhis correct, Nanda Raj Jaat-NOT Gonds, Wari-Warkari-NOT Santhals) per lesson-3 tight-cluster composite rule.

42.resolved_note: Drafted gap_changpa_community — Ladakh (NOT Uttarakhand trap), Pashmina-goat herders, ST status. Candidate era: contemporary.

45.resolved_note: Drafted gap_bnhs — founded 1883, registered NGO (NOT autonomous MoEFCC body — trap), conservation research + public education. needs_source=true for later verification.

missing_concepts: Agaria salt-pan workers of Gujarat (Little Rann of Kutch, salt-harvesting caste) — distinct from the Central-Indian Agaria iron-smelting community
51.note: PYQ tests Gujarat salt-pan Agaria. Our node covers the homonymous Central-Indian iron-smelter Agaria — different community.

55.resolved_note: Konark Sun Temple is mentioned as an Odisha Kalinga-school exemplar but there's no dedicated node; the signature chakra-wheel iconography (the specific inspiration for the logo) is not described anywhere. Distractors Hampi, Mamallapuram, Khajuraho all have dedicated nodes.

missing_concepts: Vande Mataram — composition by Bankim Chatterjee (Anandamath, 1882), original language
National Calendar of India — Saka era basis and adoption
National Flag — adoption by Constituent Assembly (22 July 1947)
Jana Gana Mana — adoption as National Anthem (Constituent Assembly, 24 January 1950)
59.note: Four-option national-symbols adoption cluster; none of the specific adoption/origin facts are in dedicated nodes. Answer (a) hinges on Vande Mataram's original language.

64.resolved_note: Three of four era-epochs explicitly in nodes: Vikrama 58/57 BCE, Shaka 78 CE, Gupta 319-320 CE. The Kali era epoch 3102 BCE (Kaliyuga commencement per the Mahabharata tradition; used in Aryabhata's astronomical reckoning) has no node.

65.resolved_note: Pre-flip: no Bhaskara I node; Aryabhata and Varahamihira were present in era graph, but the 'Bhaskara I' distractor had no counter-context to rule out.

66.resolved_note: Puhar/Kaveripattanam (=Poompuhar) and Muziris (=Muchiri) have dedicated port-nodes. Korkai — the Pandyan pearl port on the Tamraparni — is not a standalone node; the Cholas/Cheras/Pandyas node names only Madurai, Uraiyur, Puhar, Vanji, and Muziris.

67.resolved_note: Hoysalas are dated 1026-1346 in hist_hoysalas (clearly NOT 8c). Gahadavalas of Kanauj, Kakatiyas of Warangal, and Yadavas of Devagiri have no dedicated dynasty nodes — a student can't confirm any of these post-10c dynasties' founding dates directly from the graph. The Kakatiya Ramappa UNESCO node and Malik Kafur mention place Kakatiyas/Yadavas in the Khalji period but don't establish founding dates.

68.resolved_note: Answer is (d) 2 and 3 — both Chandraketugarh (Sunga-era terracotta art, West Bengal) and Ganeshwar (copper hoard site, Rajasthan, ~2800 BCE) are correctly matched, but neither has a dedicated node. Burzahom's pair-1 (rock-cut shrines) is correctly refuted by hist_burzahom + hist_pit_houses.

70.resolved_note: Missing dedicated nodes for Sohgaura (the correct answer — early Mauryan copper-plate site near Gorakhpur, NOT Harappan), Kot Diji (Early Harappan site in Sindh), and Desalpur (minor Harappan site in Kutch). Without a Sohgaura node, the graph can't explain why this answer is correct.

71.resolved_note: No node explicitly states the absence of grand palaces/temples in the IVC — a key distinguishing feature from contemporaneous Mesopotamia. Student has to infer from citadel + great-bath descriptions.

75.resolved_note: Missing explicit node on Rigvedic warfare equipment (coat of mail and helmet) — statement 1 rests on this specific claim. Currently inferable only from general Vedic-warfare nodes.

76.resolved_note: Image worship (option b distractor) has no dedicated node — image/murti worship is a post-Vedic Gupta/bhakti-era development whose absence in early Vedic isn't explicitly stated.

77.resolved_note: Missing dedicated node on Rta (Rigvedic cosmic order / fundamental moral law governing the universe). Dharma has peripheral coverage via dharmasutras/manusmriti but not as a Vedic concept.

79.resolved_note: Answer is Kosa (treasury — the odd one out among three lineage terms). Missing dedicated nodes for Vamsa (lineage), Kula (clan — appears only as 'kulapa' in period descriptions), and especially Kosa (treasury, fiscal vocabulary) — so the student can't see why Kosa is categorically different.

83.resolved_note: Khajuraho-Bundelkhand pair is clearly supported (Chandellas of Bundelkhand). Bodh Gaya, Nasik, and Malwa (Paramara) have nodes. But Shirdi (Sai Baba, Ahmednagar/Maharashtra) has no node, and the regional geographical labels — Baghelkhand, Bundelkhand, Vidarbha, Malwa, Rayalaseema — are not named/defined as geographical regions in the graph.

84.note: Buddhism node names the kingdoms of Buddha's activity ('spread rapidly via Magadha, Koshala, Kaushambi monarchies'). Buddha node places Buddha's major geography in the mid-Gangetic plain. Avanti (central India — Ujjain) and Gandhara (NW) were outside Buddha's preaching circuit. Mahajanapadas node lists all four as distinct states.

85.resolved_note: Taxila node calls it a 'Mauryan provincial capital' and 'gateway to the northwest' but does not pinpoint its Indus-Jhelum doab location. Alexander-invasion node positions Porus 'of the Jhelum-Chenab doab' (so Taxila is west of Jhelum) but does not anchor Taxila between Indus and Jhelum.

86.note: Buddha (~567-487 BCE), Bimbisara (544-492 BCE), and Prasenjit (of Kosala, contemporary of Buddha and Bimbisara — named in Ajatasattu node as 'Prasenajit of Kashi-Koshala') are 6th-5th BCE contemporaries. Menander (Milinda) is placed at c. 165-130 BCE by the Menander node — clearly the odd one out.

89.resolved_note: Rajukas have a dedicated district-level node. Pradeshika and Yukta (also district/subordinate officers named in the edicts) have no standalone nodes; the Mauryan-administration node covers central (mantri-parishad) and provincial (kumaras at Tosali/Ujjain/Taxila/Suvarnagiri) levels but does not explicitly list Pradeshika and Yukta.

90.resolved_note: Arthashastra node covers the text's scope (statecraft, 15 books, 27 adhyakshas, taxes, mandala theory) but does not state the specific slavery provisions the question tests: judicial-punishment slavery, and the rules governing dasi who bore the master's son. Student cannot evaluate the three statements from nodes alone.

91.note: Dhamma node explicitly states 'amity between sects' as a key injunction and cites the Kandahar Greek inscription preaching inter-sectarian amity. The quoted passage matches Major Rock Edict XII on religious toleration. The three distractor rulers all have nodes.

92.resolved_note: Statement 1 (Brihadratha-Pushyamitra) is explicit in Pushyamitra node. Statement 2 implicit: Shunga node says 'overthrown by their own brahmana ministers, the Kanvas' and Kanva node names Vasudeva Kanva as founder — but the last Shunga's name 'Devabhuti' is not in any node. Statement 3 explicit in Satavahana node ('defeated the Kanvas ~28 BCE'; 'called Andhras in the Puranas').

94.resolved_note: Assertion A (Ashoka annexed Kalinga) explicitly in Kalinga-war node: 'Kalinga was annexed and retained'. Reason R (Kalinga controlled land + sea routes to South India) is the standard textbook economic-strategic motive, but no node states this — Kalinga-war node focuses on casualties and Ashoka's remorse, not trade-route geography.

96.resolved_note: This is a map-based question; decision depends on the actual map image (not available in node text). Textual clues: Mauryan-empire node gives Ashoka's extent ('virtually entire subcontinent except Kerala, Tamil Nadu, NE'); Kanishka node gives 'Bactria to Pataliputra, Aral Sea to Narmada'; Samudragupta/Harsha nodes give their extents. Nodes cover all four candidate empires — the map-reading element itself remains outside the graph.

98.resolved_note: Pre-flip: 3-4c CE pivot to SE Asia trade (post-Roman, post-Hun) had no dedicated node — Suvarnabhumi context missing.

99.note: Indo-Greeks node opens: 'Greek dynasties ruling NW India from Bactria after c. 200 BCE'. Distractor options (Scythia — Shakas, Zedrasia, Aria) are regional names; Bactria is the direct answer.

100.resolved_note: Node evidence confirms the premise: Menander/Kanishka were Buddhist patrons; Shakas were 'assimilated as fallen kshatriyas' per Manusmriti — hinting at the caste-rigidity problem. The specific rationale tested ('Buddhism provided easier access to Indian society' because of its open admission across castes) is partly inferable from Buddhism node's 'accepting all castes and women into the sangha', but not framed as the reason foreign rulers chose Buddhism over Hinduism.

102.resolved_note: Kulyavapa and dronavapa are Gupta-era land-measurement units (seed-sowing-based area units) used extensively in copper-plate land grants of eastern India. No node defines them. Land-grants node describes the institution but not its measurement vocabulary.

103.resolved_note: Ghantasala (AP coast), Kadura (Karnataka coast), and Chaul (Konkan, near Alibag) were Gupta-era foreign-trade ports — none is in the graph. Indo-Roman-trade node names Broach/Bhrigukaccha, Muziris, Puhar etc. but not these.

104.resolved_note: Vishti — forced/unpaid labour levied by the state in lieu of tax, widespread in the Gupta age and described in Gupta-era inscriptions and by Fa Xian — has no node. Gupta-empire node does not list Vishti. (An Ahom-paiks node exists in era 5 but that is a different institution.)

106.note: Fa Xian (399-414 CE) and Fourth Council (c. 72-100 CE under Kanishka) are chronologically irreconcilable — nodes provide both dates, so Statement 1 is refutable. Harshavardhana node explicitly states he 'converted to Mahayana Buddhism under Xuanzang's influence' — refutes Statement 2's claim of antagonism.

107.resolved_note: Reason R (feudal expansion in Gupta period) is strongly supported — Samantas node: 'emerged as a distinct political class from Gupta times'; Land-grants node names Guptas as a key scaling phase. Assertion A (feudal origins in military campaigns) is only partially supported — land grants were pioneered by the Satavahanas as brahmana grants (not military), so the 'military campaign origin' framing is contested. Nodes do not directly rebut A but also do not support it as stated.

108.resolved_note: Tamralipti is named in Uttarapatha node as the eastern terminus of the great trunk road at the Gangetic delta — confirming it as the major north-Indian port. Fa Xian node mentions it (he embarked from Tamralipti for Sri Lanka). Bharuch (Broach, distractor) has its own node as a west-coast port. Kalyan (Konkan) and Cambray/Khambhat (Gujarat) distractors have no nodes.

110.resolved_note: Sushruta node explicitly places him as the foundational Sanskrit surgeon. Shudraka (distractor) has a node (as playwright). Saumilla and Shaunaka distractors have no nodes — both are obscure figures, Shaunaka is a Vedic ritualist of Shunga-era.

111.note: Bhasa node: 'Uses Prakrit dialogue for lower-class characters and women, as became standard.' Mrichchakatika node confirms the convention. Pali is specifically Buddhist scriptural Prakrit. Shauraseni (option d) is one variety of Prakrit, so the more general 'Prakrit' answer (b) is correct.

113.note: Pulakesin II node explicitly states: 'Decisively defeated Harshavardhana at the Narmada river c. 618 CE' — and is commemorated in the Aihole Inscription. Direct answer. Other options (Pulakesin I, Vikramaditya I, Vikramaditya II) are other Chalukyan rulers — no dedicated nodes but the context is settled.

114.resolved_note: Harshavardhana node supports both A ('held grand religious assemblies at Kanauj and Prayag') and R ('converted to Mahayana Buddhism under Xuanzang's influence'). However, deciding that R is NOT the correct explanation of A requires knowing the Prayag assembly was quinquennial mahamoksha-parishad — general charity/redistribution, not a Mahayana-only evangelism — which the nodes do not explicitly say.

115.resolved_note: Mattavilasa is attested in hist_mahendravarman_i as his Sanskrit farce (Mattavilasa Prahasana) — that alone identifies him among the options. The titles Vichitrachitta ('curious-minded') and Gunabhara ('virtue-bearing'), both known from the Mandagapattu inscription, are not in any node. Simhavarman (early Pallava predecessor, distinct from Narasimhavarman) also lacks a node.

122.resolved_note: Three of four pairs map cleanly to existing nodes (Gupta-Deogarh, Chandella-Khajuraho, Chalukya-Badami). Pallava-Panamalai has no node — Panamalai Talagirishvara is a lesser-known Pallava temple and isn't mentioned in hist_pallavas or hist_pallava_temple_stages details.

123.resolved_note: Manigramam-Nanadesi node (era 4) defines Manigramam as a south-Indian merchant guild — answers the PYQ. Shrenis node covers merchant/artisan guilds generally. Distractors have no nodes: Chaturvedimangalam (brahmadeya settlement of Vedic brahmanas under Cholas), Parishad (council of advisers — context in Mauryan-administration node as mantri-parishad), Ashtadikgaja (the mythical 8 elephants guarding the cardinal directions — not an institution).

124.resolved_note: Nannuka-Chandella and Nagabhata II-Pratihara pairs are supported. Bhoja-Rashtrakuta is eliminable since the graph identifies Mihira Bhoja as Pratihara and Bhoja Paramara of Malwa (neither Rashtrakuta). Jayashakti (a later Chandella king) has no dedicated node, so the 'Jayashakti-Paramar' incorrect pairing can't be positively refuted from the graph.

128.resolved_note: Answer is (b) 2 and 3. Inamgaon-Maharashtra-Chalcolithic is covered by hist_inamgaon. Mangadu (Kerala megalithic site) has no dedicated node — hist_megaliths only gives generic regional coverage. Distractor 1 (Chandraketugarh is West Bengal, NOT Odisha — trading port claim itself is correct for the right state) and distractor 4 (Salihundam is an Andhra Pradesh Buddhist stupa complex, NOT rock-cut cave shrines) both lack clarifying nodes.

129.resolved_note: Besnagar is correctly identified in hist_heliodorus_pillar as the Vaishnava/Bhagavata site (NOT Shaivite) — the Heliodorus Pillar is dedicated to Vasudeva/Vishnu. Sittanavasal is explicitly Jain. Bhaja Caves (Buddhist rock-cut at Pune, Maharashtra) have no dedicated node — only incidental mention in hist_barabar_caves as a chaitya-tradition descendant.

132.resolved_note: Ashokan-inscriptions node classifies edicts and names Dhauli/Jaugada as Separate-Rock-Edict sites but does not give state locations. The question is a location-matching drill — missing standalone nodes for the four sites (Dhauli-Odisha, Jaugada-Odisha, Erragudi-AP, Kalsi-Uttarakhand).

133.resolved_note: Graph establishes Somnath as a temple targeted by Mahmud of Ghazni and Al-Biruni as his scholar-companion who wrote Kitab-ul-Hind. But (i) Somnath as one of the 12 Jyotirlingas is not stated; (ii) Al-Biruni's specific description of the Somnath temple isn't quoted; (iii) the modern rebuilding / 1951 Pran Pratishtha (done by President Rajendra Prasad, not Radhakrishnan) has no node — so statement 3's falsification requires external knowledge.

134.resolved_note: Pre-flip: Ajanta-Waghora, Amaravati-Krishna (not Godavari), Sanchi-Vidisha hill (not Chambal), and Pandu-Lena (Nashik)-Godavari catchment — all four geographic pairings lacked explicit river/site nodes.

137.resolved_note: Kanganahalli (Kalaburagi district, Karnataka) — Buddhist stupa site with a unique relief-sculpture of Ashoka labelled 'Ranyo Asoko' — is not in the graph. Ashoka node lists Maski/Gujarra/Nittur/Udegolam as personal-name sites (MRE I) but not Kanganahalli's portrait inscription. Sohgaura and Shahbazgarhi (distractors) — Sohgaura has no node (flagged earlier in PYQ 70); Shahbazgarhi surfaces inside Ashokan-inscriptions as a Kharoshthi Major-Rock-Edict site.

140.resolved_note: James Prinsep is explicitly credited with deciphering Ashokan edicts in both the Ashokan-inscriptions node ('Deciphered by James Prinsep 1837') and his own biographical node. William Jones distractor covered. Georg Bühler and Max Müller (the other two distractors) are not in the graph.

142.resolved_note: All four era anchors are in the graph. Chronology is derivable (Ashokan Dhauli 3c BCE < Udayagiri 5c < Mamallapuram 7c < Lingaraja 11c). However, the specific 'rock-cut elephant sculpture at Dhauli' is not explicitly described in hist_ashokan_inscriptions — Dhauli is mentioned only as a Separate Rock Edict site.

143.resolved_note: Arjuna's Penance / Descent of Ganga at Mamallapuram is explicitly covered. Ajanta and Mount Abu (Dilwara) have nodes. The Udayagiri Caves (Gupta-era MP, site of the iconic Varaha rescuing Goddess Earth relief — the sculpture in pair 2) has no node; without it a student can't verify that Varaha is at Udayagiri, not Mount Abu. Also the specific Buddha Mahaparinirvana composition (Cave 26 Ajanta or elsewhere) isn't spelled out in hist_ajanta_paintings.

144.resolved_note: Tabo (Spiti) and Alchi (Ladakh) covered in hist_alchi_tabo_monasteries. Lhotsava Lhakhang (the incorrectly-paired one with Zanskar) has no node — student can't verify its actual location.

145.note: Viharas node: 'shelters for Buddhist and Jain monks'. Karle Chaitya node: 'sacred prayer hall'. The functional distinction — chaitya as worship hall (with apsidal stupa), vihara as monastic dwelling — is clear from these nodes.

147.resolved_note: Ajanta murals explicitly covered. Sanchi node describes sculpted gateways — no mural tradition noted, consistent with rejecting Sanchi. Lepakshi Veerabhadra temple (Vijayanagara-era, c. 16th CE, famous for ceiling murals) has no node — it is a later-era topic but the PYQ surfaces it as a correct answer.

149.resolved_note: The answer Bagh Caves (Gupta-period rock-cut Buddhist caves in Madhya Pradesh, famous for Gupta murals alongside Ajanta) has no node. Distractors Ajanta, Ellora, Lomas Rishi (Barabar), Nasik all have nodes.

150.resolved_note: The answer (Hampi Virupaksha) is covered. Distractors Bhadrachalam (AP, Rama temple) and Srikalahasti (AP, Shiva temple) have no nodes — cross-ref temple-town concepts a student may want.

missing_concepts: Vidyashankara Temple (Sringeri, Karnataka — 14c Vijayanagara Adi Shankara shrine)
Rajarani Temple (Bhubaneswar, Odisha — 11c Kalinga-style with no enshrined deity)
Bhimeshwara Temple (Draksharama, East Godavari AP — one of the Pancharama Kshetras)
152.note: Kandariya Khajuraho MP covered; the other three temple-state pairings not atomised.

153.resolved_note: Palitana Jain temples (Shatrunjaya Hill, Gujarat) and Bhavnagar have no nodes — the answer concept is absent. Distractors Mount Abu (Dilwara), Nasik (caves), Ujjain all have nodes.

154.resolved_note: Hampi answer supported via hist_hampi ('sacred centre: Virupaksha + Vitthala temples'). Belur distractor covered by Hoysala nodes. Srirangam only appears obliquely in Ramanuja's detail; Bhadrachalam and the Vitthala temple itself have no dedicated nodes.

156.resolved_note: Amaravati-Andhra Pradesh pair confirmed (answer). Udayagiri-Caves-MP node correctly places them in Madhya Pradesh (PYQ's 'Maharashtra' is the trap). Vikramshila (Bihar, Pala monastic university) and Hemkund (Uttarakhand, Sikh gurudwara) have no nodes — both are distractors so Vikramshila especially would merit a node as a famous Buddhist mahavihara.

157.resolved_note: Tabo is covered in hist_alchi_tabo_monasteries (Spiti/HP). The other three monasteries — Dhankar (HP/Spiti), Rumtek (Sikkim), and Kye/Key (HP/Spiti, the answer-pair which is incorrectly matched to Arunachal) — have no nodes. A student can't confidently eliminate the wrong pair from the graph.

159.note: Harishena node explicitly links 'Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription, c. 350 CE)' to Samudragupta. All three distractor rulers have nodes.

160.resolved_note: CST WHS has a dedicated UNESCO-tagged node. Mamallapuram and Konark have era-4 temple/architecture nodes but are not explicitly flagged as UNESCO WHS sites in the graph (both inscribed 1984). Champaner-Pavagadh (WHS 2004) has no node at all.

162.resolved_note: Answer (a) is eliminable via hist_shravana_belagola, which correctly identifies Gommateshvara as Bahubali (not the last Tirthankara). Options (c) Chandela-Khajuraho and (d) Hoysaleshvara-Shiva also supported. Only distractor (b) 'India's largest Buddhist monastery is in Arunachal Pradesh' (Tawang) has no graph node.

170.note: Ashoka node states his personal name appears only in 'Minor Rock Edict I (Maski/Gujarra/Nittur/Udegolam)'. Maski node: 'the first edict where Ashoka's personal name "Devanampiya Asoka" was identified' — direct match for option (d).

171.resolved_note: Gandhara-art node explicitly states 'grey-blue schist stone' as the signature medium. Bharhut node describes red/brown sandstone. Mathura node uses spotted red sandstone. Mauryan-art uses polished Chunar sandstone. Nodes support green/grey schist as a Gandhara, not Bharhut, marker — student can evaluate the question against nodes. (The PYQ answer key marked 'c. Bharhut' may be anomalous; the node-evidence points to Gandhara.)

174.resolved_note: Answer (four hands) is specific Nataraja iconography not stated in hist_chola_bronze or hist_lost_wax_technique details — student gets the Chola-bronze context but can't derive the exact hand count from the graph.

176.resolved_note: Chronology (Upanishads c. 6th BCE onwards, Puranas compiled mid-1st millennium CE) is cleanly supported. Statement 1 ('no parables in Upanishads') is false — Upanishads contain famous parables (Chhandogya's Svetaketu dialogue, salt-in-water, Nachiketa-Yama) — but no node explicitly mentions parabolic content in the Upanishads.

177.resolved_note: Bhasa node lists 6 of his 13 plays (Swapnavasavadatta, Pratijnayaugandharayana, Charudatta, Urubhanga, Pancharatra, Dutavakya) but not Madhyama-vyayoga — the correct answer. No nodes for the three distractors (Kavyalankara by Bhamaha; Mahabhashya by Patanjali — Natyashastra by Bharata Muni is covered).

179.resolved_note: Correct pairs (Hammira-Mahakavya:Nayachandra Suri and Nitivakyamrita:Somadeva Suri) have no supporting nodes, so the answer cannot be established. Milindapanha is in the graph as dialogue between Menander and Nagasena — that alone allows rejection of pair 3 (attributed to Nagarjuna, wrong). Devichandragupta (by Vishakhadatta, not Bilhana) has no node; Vishakhadatta surfaces only via hist_mudrarakshasa.

181.resolved_note: Sangam-literature node mentions 'early brahmanisation' (implying varna awareness), 'warrior society' (refutes option c), and 'Roman trade + muvendar politics' (refutes option a on material culture). Option d (magical forces treated as irrational) is not directly addressable from nodes — Sangam's worldview on the supernatural isn't in the graph.

183.resolved_note: Kalidasa node confirms Chandragupta II association (statement 3 ✓). Amarasimha node places him in Chandragupta II's court — so 'Amarasimha-Harshavardhana' can be rejected. Panini node gives no dating, so rejecting 'Panini-Pushyamitra' requires external knowledge (Panini c. 5th BCE pre-Mauryan; the expected association is Patanjali-Pushyamitra, but there is no Patanjali node either).

186.resolved_note: Xuanzang node is broad (travelogue, 657 manuscripts, Nalanda studies) but does not record the specific observations tested: road safety (Xuanzang himself was robbed — so statement 1 is false), judicial ordeals by fire/water/poison (statement 2 true), ferry/barrier duties on traders (statement 3 true).

189.note: Mrichchakatika node explicitly summarises the plot: 'love of impoverished brahmana merchant Charudatta and the courtesan Vasantasena' — matches option (a). The distractor options about Chandragupta II's Shaka conquests and Samudragupta's campaigns are separately covered.

190.note: Mudrarakshasa node names Vishakhadatta as author and summarises plot as 'Chanakya's political machinations to secure Chandragupta Maurya's throne after the Nanda overthrow' — directly matches option (d) 'court intrigues at the time of Chandragupta Maurya'.

193.note: All four pairs are checkable: Mrichchakatika-Shudraka ✓, Buddhacharita-Ashvaghosha (PYQ claims Vasubandhu — refutable via Buddhacharita and Ashvaghosha nodes), Mudrarakshasa-Vishakhadatta ✓, Harshacharita-Banabhatta ✓.

197.note: Milindapanho node explicitly: 'dialogue form, recording questions put by Indo-Greek king Menander to the Buddhist monk Nagasena'. Nagarjuna distractor has its own node (Madhyamaka philosopher, 2nd-3rd CE, unrelated).

198.resolved_note: Varahamihira-Brihatsamhita pair explicit in Varahamihira node. Shudraka-Mrichchakatikam explicit. Vishakhadatta authored both Mudrarakshasa (covered) and Devichandragupta (NOT in graph — the pair Vishakhadatta-Devichandragupta tested in option II-D has no supporting node). Bilhana (Kashmiri poet who wrote Vikramankadevacharita) has no node. Merutunga's Prabandha-Chintamani (14c Jain work) has no node.
